title: Trump's Shocking Grab for Power
description_medium: An August 2026 Sydney Morning Herald opinion article criticized an Office of Legal Counsel memo asserting executive privilege over a president’s communications with private advisers outside government. The author argued that the privilege normally covers communications within government, and warned the broader view could shield private associates from congressional investigation.
description_long: An August 2026 Sydney Morning Herald opinion article examined a new Office of Legal Counsel memorandum asserting that executive privilege covers a president’s communications with private advisers who are not government officials. The author, law professor Noah Feldman, argued that the privilege traditionally protects communications within government, including exchanges between a president and public officials, rather than private conversations with outside associates. He warned that treating private advisers as covered could make it harder for Congress to investigate possible deals involving people close to the president. The article urged Congress to challenge any future assertion in court rather than accept the memo’s interpretation. It described the administration’s legal position and the risk Feldman saw in it; it did not report that a court had upheld the claim or that a particular congressional investigation had already been blocked. The dispute concerned the boundaries of executive privilege and whether a legal doctrine designed to protect government deliberations could extend to private communications. The opinion framed that expansion as a threat to congressional oversight and public accountability.
notes: The linked Sydney Morning Herald opinion identifies the memo’s claim as extending privilege to presidential communications with private advisers outside government. The article argues that this departs from the doctrine’s traditional scope and predicts a threat to congressional oversight; it does not document a court ruling or completed obstruction of a specific investigation.

title: Trump's New Crypto Bank Scandal
description_medium: A New Republic opinion article reported that the Trump family’s crypto company, World Liberty Financial, received conditional approval for a national trust bank charter in August 2026. The article said the family owned 38% of the company and received 75% of its crypto revenue. The approval was conditional, not a final charter or proof of unlawful conduct.
description_long: On August 18, 2026, The New Republic reported that the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency had conditionally approved World Liberty Financial’s application to create a national trust bank, to be called World Liberty Trust Company. The article said the Trump family owned a 38% stake in World Liberty Financial and received 75% of its crypto revenue. It also reported that Donald Trump had collected nearly $600 million from the company in the prior year, citing his financial disclosure. The conditional approval followed a broader increase in applications for national bank charters under the Trump administration; the article said final approval still depended on the company raising sufficient capital. The author argued the arrangement raised a conflict because the president’s family could benefit financially from a company receiving federal banking approval under an administration led by Trump. The article was an opinion piece criticizing the decision and describing it as self-dealing. Conditional approval was not the same as a final charter, and the report did not describe a legal finding that officials had violated banking law or improperly influenced the application.
organization_tags: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
notes: The New Republic article is an opinion piece. It reports conditional OCC approval and family ownership/revenue figures, while arguing that the approval raises conflict-of-interest concerns. The approval was not final and the article reports no legal finding of wrongdoing.

title: Trump's Secret Police Spying on Americans
description_short: Trump's Secret Police Spying on Americans
description_medium: A New Republic article described court papers from a prosecution of anti-ICE protesters that it said showed DHS agents surveilling left-leaning groups after ICE killed Alex Pretti in January 2026. The reports allegedly included infiltrated meetings, requests for financial records and, in some cases, secret recordings. The material concerns specific protest groups, not a proven nationwide surveillance program.
description_long: A New Republic article published on August 19, 2026, discussed court papers filed in the prosecution of several anti-ICE protesters. The article said the documents showed the Department of Homeland Security began surveilling left-leaning groups after ICE killed Alex Pretti in January. The reported targets included a union, a climate organization and groups such as the Sunrise Movement. The activity described in agent reports included attending protest meetings undercover, seeking financial records and, in some cases, secretly recording gatherings. One report said a Sunrise Movement meeting in Minneapolis was focused on peaceful protest. These details raise questions about how federal agencies distinguish protest activity from conduct warranting investigation, especially when the meetings described were protected by the First Amendment. The article relied on court exhibits attached to a defense motion and described operations directed at a handful of groups and protesters. It did not establish that the surveillance was ordered personally by Trump or that every monitored group was part of a single national operation. The disclosures intensified debate over whether monitoring protest meetings can chill lawful political activity and how such investigations fit with First Amendment protections.

preserved_fields.title: Trump's Secret Police Spying on Americans
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump's Secret Police Spying on Americans

notes: The New Republic article describes court exhibits alleging undercover attendance at protest meetings and requests for financial records. Its broader characterization of a Trump “secret police” operation is not established by the cited examples. Proposed correction: use a neutral title about DHS surveillance of anti-ICE groups based on court filings, and keep the scope limited to the groups and meetings described.

title: Imposes Section 201 Tariffs on Solar Panels and Washing Machines
description_short: Trump issued a proclamation imposing safeguard tariffs on imported solar cells and washing machines.
description_medium: On January 23, 2018, President Trump issued a proclamation imposing safeguard tariffs on imported solar cells and modules and large residential washing machines. The action used Section 201 trade authority. The supplied summary does not state the tariff rates, product exclusions, duration or effects on consumers and manufacturers.
organization_tags: Office of the U.S. Trade Representative

title: Terminates TPS for Haiti
description_short: DHS announced termination of Temporary Protected Status for Haiti, forcing many immigrants toward removal.
description_medium: On November 20, 2017, the Department of Homeland Security announced that it would terminate Haiti’s designation for Temporary Protected Status. The decision put the immigration protection of Haitians relying on TPS at risk and could leave them subject to removal. The supplied material does not give the number affected or the implementation timeline.
subcategory: Legal Immigration Status Revocation and Humanitarian Protection Elimination
